newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Council faces showdown on postal services.
newsitem.headline: Council faces showdown on postal services.

text.p: The European Union faces a showdown on Thursday over a Franco-German effort to delay significant liberalisation of EU postal services until at least 2003.
The proposal, which will be discussed by the Telecommunications Council, has divided the 15 EU governments and drawn the wrath of the European Commission.
"We cannot work on the basis of this compromise," Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann told a news conference on Wednesday, saying the plan violated EU law by tying the Commission's hands.

France, mindful of the strikes that paralysed the country a year ago and wary of triggering further social unrest, has led the drive to water down the Commission's effort to open postal services to competition.
In a move that has mystified Brussels officials, Germany reversed its relatively pro-liberalisation stance earlier this month and threw its weight behind the French effort.
"This is a love affair," Bangemann quipped. "Love goes to your head as it were and you lose all reason."

The controversy involves when, or if, national governments should be required to allow operators across Europe to compete with state post offices to deliver direct mail ("junk mail") and cross-border mail.

The Commission proposed in 1995 that the EU begin by allowing competitors to deliver mail weighing more than 350 grammes and with tariffs more than five times the public tariff for a standard letter -- a tiny percentage of overall traffic.
It said that direct mail and incoming cross-border mail should in principle be opened to competition on January 1, 2001, though it would decide in 1998 whether to hold to that date.
But that proposal, while timid compared with the Commission's efforts to open up the telecoms sector, proved unacceptable to countries including France, Belgium, Greece, Luxembourg and Portugal.
They argued that too many jobs were at stake and that introducing competition too quickly would lead to a deterioration of "universal service" -- basic mail delivery to all citizens.
Britain, the Nordic countries and the Netherlands, on the other hand, supported 2001, at least for direct mail.
France and Germany came up with their proposal after an inconclusive meeting of EU telecoms ministers on postal liberalisation in September.

It calls on EU ministers and the European Parliament to decide by 2001 whether to open up direct mail and cross-border mail but stipulates that the liberalisation could not actually take place before July 2003.

The pro-liberalisation countries are unhappy with the deal and will try to block it on Thursday. "We're very opposed to the Franco-German proposal because it would do nothing," a British official said.
"The way this compromise has happened has taken the others aback, the way two member states have told the others, 'eat or die'," an EU diplomat said.

The ministers are under some pressure to strike a deal since the Commission has said that it would adopt a notice on its own explaining how it would apply EU competition rules to the postal sector by the end of 1996.

Bangemann said the Franco-German proposal was illegal because it would bar the Commission from exercising powers it has under Article 90 0f the EC treaty to force governments to open up competition in the public sector. (See BC-POST-COMPETITION-BANGEMANN)
He said the Commission was willing to work on the basis of an Irish presidency compromise submitted to the September Telecommunications Council.

The Irish proposed that direct mail be liberalised by January 1, 2001 and that ministers pledge to adopt measures by that date on further liberalisation of the sector, with particular attention to incoming cross-border mail.
